did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title attributes it to the sons of Korah and includes the phrase “upon the Gittith”; the psalm itself expresses longing for the house of the LORD and closeness to Him.
Did you know? The phrase “How lovely are your dwelling places” opens the psalm by expressing love and wonder at the places where the LORD dwells.
Did you know? Longing for the house of the LORD is described as involving both body and soul: “my heart and flesh” sing for joy to the “living God.”
Did you know? The psalm uses a bird that has found a home and a sparrow that has found a nest as images of one seeking a permanent place near the LORD’s altars.
Did you know? The word “blessed” appears twice in the psalm: here, it describes the happiness of those who dwell in the LORD’s house, and later, the happiness of the person who trusts in Him.
Did you know? According to the verse, a person’s strength is found in the LORD, and the hearts of those who go up to Him are set on “highways”—a road or path leading to the destination.
Did you know? Even the “Valley of Baca,” described in the psalm as a place of passage, becomes a place of springs and blessings; this portrays a journey in which hardship and blessing come together.
Did you know? The ascent is described as a process of continual progress: “from strength to strength,” until appearing before God in Zion.
Did you know? In this prayer, the psalmist asks the LORD to hear his prayer, look upon “our shield,” and behold the face of “your anointed”—an expression linking protection with messianic leadership.
Did you know? The psalmist would rather stand at the threshold of the house of God than dwell in the tents of wickedness, and considers one day in the LORD’s courts better than a thousand elsewhere.
